detail.extracted_title: Navigating Centuries in Ink: Inside Oman's Guest of Honour Pavilion at the Sharjah Book Fair
detail.excerpt: Designed in the silhouette of a traditional dhow sail, Oman's Guest of Honour pavilion at the 45th Sharjah International Book Fair unites 42 institutions and publishers with rare manuscripts dating back to 1137 CE.
detail.article_html:
At the entrance to the Sultanate of Oman's Guest of Honour pavilion at the 45th Sharjah International Book Fair, visitors pass beneath an architectural structure shaped like the taut triangular sail of a traditional Omani dhow. The design is an intentional prelude to what lies inside: a centuries-old intellectual tradition in which sea routes, astronomical logs, courtroom ledgers, and handwritten codices connected the ports of Oman to the wider Indian Ocean and the Arab world.

Inaugurated by His Highness Sheikh Dr. Sultan bin Muhammad Al-Qasimi, Ruler of Sharjah, alongside an Omani delegation led by His Highness Sayyid Saud bin Hilal Al-Busaidi, Minister of Culture, Sports and Youth, Oman's participation brings together 25 government and civil society institutions, 17 Omani publishing houses, and a cultural program encompassing 82 literary, historical, and artistic events. During the opening tour, Sayyid Saud bin Hilal Al-Busaidi presented the Ruler of Sharjah with The Encyclopedia of the Omani Empire from the Coasts of Africa to the Coasts of India, setting the tone for a showcase anchored in primary historical documentation.

Rare Manuscripts of Jurisprudence, Medicine, and the Sea

At the heart of the Omani pavilion sits a curated treasury of original manuscripts that trace the breadth of Omani scholarship across nearly a millennium. Among the earliest works on display is Al-Muharaba, a treatise by the jurist Bashir bin Mohammed bin Mahboub regarded as one of the oldest surviving works in Islamic political jurisprudence, notable for its early marginal annotations referencing historical events. Nearby rests Majmu' fi Al-Siyar wal-Jawabat, a compilation of biographical epistles and legal responses copied in 531 AH (1137 CE) that ranks among the oldest dated historical manuscripts preserved in Oman.

Scientific and maritime scholarship occupy an equally prominent place. Visitors can examine Ma'din Al-Asrar fi 'Ilm Al-Bihar (The Mine of Secrets in the Science of the Seas), the landmark navigational manual authored by Omani master navigator Nasser bin Ali Al-Khadhouri, which was inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2017. Beside it lies a rare medical treatise by the Omani physician Rashid bin Umayrah Al-Hashimi Al-Ayni Al-Rustaqi, who practiced between the tenth and eleventh centuries AH, alongside Mushaf Al-Qira'at Al-Sab' (Codex of the Seven Readings), calligraphed in the twelfth century AH by Sheikh Abdullah bin Bashir Al-Hadhrami.

Travel literature is represented by Tanzih Al-Absar, an eyewitness chronicle documenting the four-month, eighteen-day diplomatic voyage of Sultan Barghash bin Said from Zanzibar to Britain in 1292 AH (1875 CE). Together, these manuscripts demonstrate how Omani scholars wrote simultaneously for the mosque, the clinic, the courtroom, and the quarterdeck.

Muttrah's Court Ledgers and Shared Gulf Maritime Memory

One of the pavilion's most resonant historical releases speaks directly to the shared kinship between Oman and the United Arab Emirates. Published by the Oman Memory Centre and compiled by researcher Badr bin Saif Al-Rajhi, the book Asma' Al-Nawakhiydha (Names of the Ship Captains) extracts archival records from the Sharia Court of Muttrah between 1353 and 1356 AH (1934 to 1937 CE).

Those judicial registers preserve the names, commercial transactions, and maritime disputes of ship captains (nawakhiydha) from the coast of the United Arab Emirates who anchored and traded regularly in Muttrah Harbor during the 1930s. Far from ceremonial rhetoric, the court entries capture the everyday legal and commercial trust that bound Gulf seafaring families together generations before modern borders.

Eighty-Two Events Bridging Oral Storytelling and Modern Publishing

Beyond its archival display cases, the pavilion functions as an active forum for contemporary Omani writers, translators, and researchers. A dedicated program of 28 intellectual seminars and 54 cultural and artistic activities explores everything from the oral sea tales (al-hikayat al-bahriyya) of Musandam, Batinah, Sur, and Dhofar to modern Omani short fiction, children's picture books, and green chemistry.

Digital preservation also takes center stage through the Ministry of Information's Ayn platform for audiobooks and digital publications, alongside a virtual reality exhibition displaying twelve Omani fine-art paintings inspired by rock art and architectural ornamentation. Whether through a twelfth-century CE manuscript or an interactive children's storytelling workshop, Oman's pavilion in Sharjah affirms that a nation's stories endure when its archives remain open to new readers.

detail.instagram_caption:
Beneath an entrance shaped like the triangular sail of an Omani dhow, the Sultanate of Oman has opened its Guest of Honour pavilion at the 45th Sharjah International Book Fair. Bringing together 25 government and civil society institutions, 17 Omani publishing houses, and 82 cultural events, the pavilion traces nearly nine centuries of Omani writing across jurisprudence, medicine, navigation, and literature.

Visitors can view original manuscripts including Majmu' fi Al-Siyar wal-Jawabat copied in 531 AH (1137 CE), Nasser Al-Khadhouri's UNESCO-registered maritime manual Ma'din Al-Asrar fi 'Ilm Al-Bihar, and Tanzih Al-Absar, which chronicles Sultan Barghash bin Said's 1875 voyage from Zanzibar to Britain. Meanwhile, a new archival volume from the Oman Memory Centre documents UAE ship captains (nawakhiydha) recorded in the Sharia Court ledgers of Muttrah between 1934 and 1937, revealing the everyday commercial bonds that connected Gulf ports.

Which chapter of Oman's manuscript and maritime heritage would you most like to explore first?
